title: Ministerial duties, statutory discretion, and the Take Care Clause
shortTitle: Ministerial duties, statutory discretion, and the Take Care Clause
summary: A ministerial duty requires an official to perform a legally specified act; presidential supervision does not authorize an official to contradict a valid statutory command.
notes:
A ministerial duty is a legally prescribed act whose required performance does not depend on the official’s policy preference. A discretionary power permits judgment within a range the law leaves open. The reading uses this distinction to explain why executive supervision and compliance with statutes pose separate questions. Section 301 of title 3 permits delegation of certain statutory presidential functions to Senate-confirmed executive officials. That authority does not establish a presidential power to disregard duties Congress placed directly on another official.

Marbury’s discussion of delivery of a signed and sealed commission treats a compulsory duty affecting individual rights as subject to mandamus. The casebook labels that discussion dicta. Little v. Barreme upheld damages against a ship captain whose presidentially ordered seizure exceeded the seizure authority Congress supplied. Kendall rejected the Postmaster General’s reliance on presidential direction to resist a payment commanded by statute. Together, the cases support the proposition that the obligation faithfully to execute law does not confer a general power to suspend it.

The difficult question concerns choices within a genuine statutory range. William Wirt’s 1823 opinion emphasized Congress’s assignment of a function to a named official and denied presidential substitution. Roger Taney’s Princess of Orange opinion allowed presidential direction of a prosecutor already authorized to discontinue a suit, with removal as a response to refusal. The editors distinguish the institutional settings and identify a still-contested question about directing lawful policy discretion. Sierra Club v. Costle supports presidential policy involvement absent a legal restriction, but an agency must still supply a legally adequate explanation. The classroom bilingual-education hypothetical makes that boundary concrete: a statute prioritizing educational efficacy regardless of cost cannot be implemented under a presidential instruction that substitutes cost effectiveness regardless of efficacy.
